newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: China's Uighur riot continues, say exiles.
newsitem.headline: China's Uighur riot continues, say exiles.

text.p: Leaders of an exiled nationalist Uighur group in Kazakhstan said on Friday that riots in China's predominantly Moslem north-west were continuing despite Beijing's statement that disturbances had been quelled.

"We are sure, and there are facts proving this, that it is too early for Beijing to announce that the riots have been neutralised," Yusupbek Mukhlisi, leader of the United National Front of Turkestan, told a news conference.

"The riots go on in several areas of the province of Xinjiang where people have taken up arms to defend themselves, but Beijing has managed to create an information vacuum around the event," Mukhlisi said in the Kazakh capital Almaty.

Chinese officials said on Thursday the riot in the town of Yining, 50 km (30 miles) from the border with Kazakhstan, that started last week, had been "fomented by hostile foreign forces" but had finally been quelled by the army and police.
Chinese officials have said nine people were killed and at least 198 wounded, including about 50 of them seriously.
But Mukhlisi said that the real death toll in Yining was betweeen 80 and 90 between February 5 and 10 alone.
Beijing says the riot had erupted after an Uighur criminal suspect resisted arrest by police.
Officials said that about 1,000 people, mostly Uighur farmers and unemployed youths, rampaged through Yining, smashing and burning cars, looting shops and demanding China's pullout from the province.
But Mukhlisi said the riot had been triggered by "Beijing's colonial policy, genocide, mass influx of ethnic Han Chinese to the province and social-economic problems of the Uighurs".
Turkic-speaking Uighurs are in the majority in Xinjiang, where ethnic Han Chinese make up 38 percent of the population.
Mukhlisi said last week's execution of 30 Uighur nationalists was the last straw. "The knife has finally cut the bone," he said.
Mukhlisi said that since April 1996 some 57,000 Uighur separatists had been arrested and about 1,700 of them executed.

Last week's riot was one of the largest, most violent demonstrations for independence in the mainly Moslem region of Xinjiang -- which means New Frontier in Chinese -- since the 1949 communist takeover.
Another Uighur leader, Kakhriman Kozhamberdi, said: "The recent riot and reprisals against Chinese Moslems regretfully, drew no reaction from heads of the Central Asian region."
Leaders of ex-Soviet republics bordering China have kept a diplomatic silence during the latest disturbances.
